overview: Dexus (ASX: DXS) is a leading Australasian fully integrated real asset group that owns, manages and develops office, industrial, retail, healthcare and infrastructure assets. It operates a stapled structure combining a $15.3 billion directly-owned listed investment portfolio with a $36.1 billion third-party funds management business, together forming a $51.4 billion 'Dexus Platform', plus a $12.8 billion real estate development pipeline. The group operates across Australia and New Zealand, earning income from property rents, co-investment stakes in pooled funds, funds management fees, and development/trading profits.

business_model.summary: Dexus earns recurring rental income from its owned office and industrial portfolio (~76% of FFO), supplemented by co-investment income from pooled funds, funds management fees (base + performance fees on $36.1bn third-party AUM), and episodic trading/development profits. It is structured as a stapled entity (Dexus Property Trust + Dexus Operations Trust) required to distribute the large majority of AFFO (80-100% payout policy).
business_model.customer_type: B2B - corporate and government office tenants, industrial/logistics tenants, and institutional third-party capital partners (pension funds, sovereign wealth funds) in funds management vehicles
business_model.geographic_mix: Australia (Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide, Canberra) and New Zealand; predominantly Sydney and Melbourne CBD office plus east-coast industrial/logistics

competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest ASX-listed diversified real asset managers by portfolio value ($51.4bn Platform), with a top-tier office and industrial direct portfolio and a sizeable third-party funds management franchise; historically a top-3 Australian office landlord, though recently ceding scale through asset recycling and fund reviews

moat_factors.description: Deep sector expertise, development capability and active asset management across office/industrial/retail/healthcare gives access to third-party capital and co-investment opportunities that smaller managers cannot replicate
$36.1bn of third-party FUM generates recurring base management fees plus performance fees, though this is currently under pressure from the AMP Capital infrastructure fund reviews
Premium CBD towers (e.g., Quay Quarter Tower Sydney) and modern logistics estates support above-average occupancy (95.7% office, 94.6% industrial) versus national average vacancy of ~14-16%
A-/A3 credit rating, $2.5bn liquidity and diversified debt sources support access to capital through cycles

weaknesses: Reputational damage and governance failures exposed by the APAC (Melbourne/Launceston Airports) litigation loss, which found a 'material Irremediable Breach' of a shareholders' deed and could force a distressed sale of a ~27%-owned $4.5bn stake
Ten-year total shareholder return of just 0.2% p.a., materially underperforming the AREIT index (5.7% p.a.), reflecting weak long-run capital allocation and execution
Funds management franchise under strategic review across $7.3bn of infrastructure FUM (~$35m of fee income) with client redemptions/consultations underway, creating earnings uncertainty into FY27
Heavy office weighting (54% of FFO) exposed to structurally elevated vacancy and slower-than-hoped recovery outside prime CBD assets
Securities trading at a steep discount to NTA ($8.95/security book value vs. ~$5.7-6.9 traded price), indicating market skepticism about asset values or execution credibility

growth_drivers: On-market buyback of up to 10% of securities funded by asset sale proceeds, directly accretive given the large discount to NTA
Asset recycling program ($2.5bn divested over two years, ahead of schedule) redeploying capital into higher-return industrial and funds co-investment opportunities

Boral logistics estate partnership in Melbourne's western corridor - potential to create one of Australia's largest logistics estates (up to 2.5m sqm lettable area) via a capital-efficient, phased, third-party-capital-backed development model
Growth in funds management third-party capital raising (~$2.0bn raised in FY26, including $260m in the final two months) as investor sentiment in core real estate improves

Flight-to-quality leasing dynamics in Australian office markets - limited new CBD supply through 2026-28 supporting rental growth for prime assets like Quay Quarter Tower and the Atlassian Sydney HQ (completing late 2026)
Stabilising/declining capitalisation rates lifting investment property valuations after several years of cap-rate-driven writedowns
Platform efficiency and cost discipline initiatives, including AI tool adoption, workforce right-sizing, and fund rationalisation to improve margins

business.risk: APAC litigation and forced stake sale
business.description: NSW Supreme Court found Dexus (as manager of the 'Dexus Bloc', ~27% of Melbourne/Launceston Airports owner APAC) committed a material irremediable breach of the shareholders' deed by leaking confidential data-room information to GIC and Mubadala during a stake sale process; Dexus faces a forced sale of the ~$4.5bn holding, is funding investors' appeal costs and adverse cost orders, and the ultimate financial impact on Dexus remains uncertain pending appeal

business.risk: Funds management client attrition and fund reviews
business.description: Strategic review of infrastructure funds/mandates from the 2023 AMP Capital transaction ($7.3bn FUM, ~$35m fees) may result in restructuring, consolidation or liquidation; increased redemption queue at the $1.1bn Dexus Healthcare Property Fund also signals investor caution
Hybrid/WFH work patterns continue to elevate national office vacancy (13.9-16.1% depending on market/measure), pressuring secondary assets even as prime CBD stock benefits from flight-to-quality
Management has flagged FY27 AFFO will be lower than FY26 due to minimal performance fees, materially lower trading profits, higher finance costs, and a reduced contribution from FUM under review

financial.description: Look-through gearing rose from 31.7% (FY25) to 33.9-34.2% at Dec-2025/FY26, still within the 30-40% target band but moving toward the upper half amid asset revaluation swings and buyback funding needs

Weighted average cost of debt increased from 4.2% to 4.7% over the half; while 95% of debt is hedged (limiting near-term rate risk), refinancing at higher rates will pressure net finance costs over time

Statutory earnings are highly volatile due to derivative and investment property fair-value swings (FY26 NPAT $482.2m vs FY25 $136.1m, driven almost entirely by revaluation gains/losses rather than operating performance)

regulatory.risk: AASB S2 climate disclosure compliance costs
regulatory.description: New mandatory sustainability/climate reporting standards add compliance overhead, though Dexus already reports voluntarily at a high standard

As Responsible Entity for numerous unlisted wholesale funds, Dexus carries fiduciary and conduct obligations - exactly the duty found breached in the APAC matter - creating ongoing regulatory and reputational scrutiny of its funds management conduct

macro.description: As a leveraged real asset owner, Dexus's asset valuations (via capitalisation rates), funding costs, and NTA are all sensitive to the direction of Australian interest rates; the FY26 recovery in statutory profit was driven by stabilising cap rates, a reversal that would recur adversely if rates rise again
Elevated rates and geopolitical uncertainty have slowed real asset transaction volumes, constraining the pace at which Dexus can execute its divestment program and fund the buyback
Office and industrial rental growth depend on corporate hiring and consumer/logistics demand; a broader economic slowdown would soften leasing volumes and rent reviews

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian CBD office total returns are forecast to exceed historical averages over 2026-28 on improving net effective rents and limited new supply (three of the next five years with no new Sydney completions), but the recovery is bifurcated - Melbourne CBD vacancy remains elevated (~20.5%) while Brisbane and Canberra lead the recovery. Industrial/logistics remains structurally favoured by e-commerce and supply chain trends, though the sector has matured from its post-COVID peak.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - property values and REIT earnings are strongly cyclical, driven by interest rates (via capitalisation rates), credit availability, and tenant demand; Dexus's own 10-year TSR of 0.2% p.a. illustrates the sector's post-2021 drawdown
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High - direct impact on cap rates/valuations, funding costs, and distributable income; 95% of debt is hedged near-term which dampens but does not eliminate sensitivity

recent_developments.event: FY26 results: AFFO of $483.9m (flat YoY) and distributions of 37.0 cps met guidance; statutory NPAT rose to $482.2m (FY25: $136.1m) on positive revaluation swing as cap rates stabilised; gearing rose to 33.4% (FY25: 31.7%)

Board issued FY27 guidance of AFFO 37.5-39.5 cps (a meaningful step-down from FY26's 44.5-45.5 cps range), citing lower trading profits/performance fees, higher finance costs, and reduced contribution from funds management under review

Commenced a strategic review of infrastructure funds/mandates inherited from the 2023 AMP Capital transaction ($7.3bn third-party FUM, ~$35m in management fees), with advisers appointed and consultation underway with 70+ investor parties

NSW Supreme Court ruled against the Dexus-managed 'Dexus Bloc' (~27% of Australia Pacific Airports Corporation, owner of Melbourne/Launceston Airports) in litigation over a botched stake-sale process involving GIC and Mubadala, finding a material irremediable breach; Dexus faces a forced sale of the ~$4.5bn stake, funding investor appeal/legal costs, and took internal disciplinary action including employee stand-downs
Announced an on-market buyback of up to 10% of securities, funded by asset sale proceeds, in response to the persistent discount between the share price and NTA
Executing the buyback in the market (e.g., 536,168 securities bought back at A$5.74-5.80), well below the $8.95 NTA per security reported at 31 Dec 2025

Raised c.$2.0bn of third-party equity into funds management (incl. $260m in the final two months of FY26); flagship Dexus Wholesale Property Fund (DWPF) delivered its strongest one-year return in almost four years
Issued A$500m of subordinated notes (callable 2031/2034) in the Australian fixed income market, diversifying funding and receiving 50% equity credit from S&P/Moody's
Board renewal: Nicola Roxon and Paula Dwyer retired as non-executive directors; Jon Gidney and Varya Davidson appointed

items.notes: Down from FY26 actual of 45.0 cents; management attributes the decline to an immaterial performance fee/trading profit contribution (vs. an elevated FY26), higher finance costs, practical completion of Atlassian Central, and a materially lower contribution from FUM under review/consultation. Guidance is subject to no material deterioration in conditions and excludes any impact from decisions not yet made on the infrastructure fund reviews
Held flat versus FY26's 37.0 cents despite lower AFFO guidance, implying a higher payout ratio

items.metric: AFFO per security (superseded FY26 guide, for reference)
items.notes: FY26 guidance reaffirmed at the H1 FY26 results and subsequently met

items.target: Up to 10% of securities on issue
items.notes: Execution tied to the pace of asset sales and capital released from the balance sheet; management describes it as 'the most direct action available' given the discount to independently assessed asset value

items.target: Continuation of program; $2.5bn achieved over FY25-FY26 (exceeding prior target)
items.notes: Proceeds directed to gearing management, buyback funding and portfolio rebalancing

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Ross Du Vernet acknowledged the FY26 security price 'does not reflect the value we believe exists in the underlying business' and highlighted a 'sustained disconnect' between the equity market valuation and underlying asset values, positioning the buyback as the most direct value-creation lever available. Management reiterated commitment to becoming a more capital-efficient, diversified business but cautioned that the shift will take time, with FY27 earnings guided lower and 'no decisions have been made' yet on the outcome of the infrastructure fund strategic review, whose resolution may await the outcome of the APAC judgment appeal.

bull_case: Securities trade at a very large discount to net tangible assets ($8.95 NTA per security vs. ~$5.7-6.9 traded price), and management is directly addressing this via a 10%-of-register buyback funded by asset sales - a highly accretive use of capital if the discount persists

Property valuations have inflected positively as capitalisation rates stabilise (office +0.7%, industrial +1.6% in H1 FY26), suggesting the multi-year devaluation cycle may be behind the sector, with CBRE/JLL forecasting above-average total returns for prime CBD office through 2026-28

High-quality, well-occupied core portfolio (95.7% office, 94.6% industrial occupancy, both above national averages) with strong rent collection (99.7%) demonstrates resilient underlying operating performance despite headline volatility

Disciplined balance sheet (A-/A3 rating, gearing at the lower end of the 30-40% target range, $2.5bn liquidity, 95% hedged debt) provides capacity to execute the buyback and withstand near-term earnings softness

Capital-efficient growth optionality via the Boral logistics partnership (up to 2.5m sqm) and continued third-party capital raising (~$2.0bn in FY26) offers a path to scale funds management without balance-sheet-heavy capex
bear_case: The APAC litigation loss is a serious governance and reputational failure - a court found a 'material Irremediable Breach' involving leaked confidential information to sovereign wealth funds, Dexus faces a forced sale of a $4.5bn stake, is funding investor legal costs, and the financial/reputational fallout (including client trust in the funds management franchise) remains unresolved pending appeal

FY27 AFFO guidance of 37.5-39.5 cents is a 12-18% step-down from FY26's 45.0 cents, showing that FY26's 'resilience' relied on an unsustainable mix of elevated trading profits and performance fees that will not repeat

Ten-year total shareholder return of just 0.2% p.a. versus the AREIT index's 5.7% p.a. is a damning long-run track record that predates but is compounded by the current governance and strategic missteps

Third-party funds management business - a key differentiator versus pure-play landlords - is under active strategic review across $7.3bn of infrastructure FUM, with redemption pressure also building in the Healthcare Property Fund, creating a multi-year overhang on fee income and platform credibility

Heavy office exposure (54% of FFO) remains vulnerable to structurally elevated vacancy outside prime assets (national CBD vacancy ~14-16%, Melbourne ~20.5%), and rising cost of debt (4.2% to 4.7% over one half) will progressively pressure net finance costs as hedges roll off
